platforms.title: 3 Signs That Separate Trigger Finger From Dupuytren's
platforms.meta_description: Finger catching when you bend it, or slowly curling toward your palm? How the ASSH tells trigger finger apart from Dupuytren's contracture.
platforms.body_html:
Does your finger catch or snap when you bend and straighten it, or is it slowly curling toward your palm and won't straighten anymore? The American Society for Surgery of the Hand (ASSH) explains that trigger finger and Dupuytren's contracture involve completely different tissue in the hand. Mixing the two up and just stretching can mean missing the treatment window that actually matters.

Why the same general problem has different causes

Trigger finger is inflammation of a tendon and the pulley it slides through, causing the finger to catch, snap, or lock when bending or straightening. A tender lump is often felt at the base of the finger in the palm, and symptoms are frequently worse first thing in the morning.

Dupuytren's contracture comes from an entirely different tissue. It's marked by the connective tissue under the skin of the palm slowly thickening and tightening, gradually pulling one or more fingers toward the palm until they can't be straightened. It's usually painless and progresses slowly over months to years, without any catching or snapping.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether there's pain, and whether the finger catches or snaps. The ASSH notes these are clear features of trigger finger, while Dupuytren's contracture is usually painless and simply curls the finger gradually without any snapping sensation.

Second, whether a firm cord or lump can be felt in the palm, and where it leads. Dupuytren's often produces a firm, cord-like band of tissue running from the palm toward the finger. Trigger finger produces a lump confined to a single point where the finger begins.

What matters most is not trying to fix Dupuytren's contracture with stretching or massage alone. The problem is the connective tissue itself thickening, so stretching doesn't loosen it, and once it progresses far enough, a needle procedure to release the tissue or surgery may be needed. Trigger finger, on the other hand, often responds well early on to splinting or a steroid injection, but if left untreated the finger can lock in a bent position and require surgery to release the pulley.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note whether there's pain, whether catching happens, the shape and location of anything felt in the palm, and how quickly the symptoms have been progressing. Left untreated, both conditions can affect finger function, so seeing a hand specialist is the safe move if it doesn't improve within a few days.

Risk factors differ between the two as well. Trigger finger is linked to repetitive gripping motions and is more common in people with diabetes, while Dupuytren's contracture is tied more to being over 40, having Northern European ancestry, a family history of the condition, and sometimes heavy alcohol use. Neither list is a diagnosis on its own, but it can help explain why the same hand issue shows up in different people for different reasons.

Taking a photo of the hand every few weeks is a simple way to track how quickly things are changing, since that kind of record gives a hand specialist a much clearer picture of the pace of progression than trying to describe it from memory during a short appointment.

Does your finger catch when you bend it, or is it painlessly curling toward your palm over time?
